title: 7 · Mnemonics and Quick Recall
learn:
• ACID: All Cars Insist on Diesel (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability).
  • Deadlock conditions MHNC: My Hungry Neighbour Cooks = Mutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No preemption, Circular wait.
  • Conflicts: W-W lost update, W-R dirty read, R-W unrepeatable read, plus incorrect summary (aggregate). Remember: Lost, Dirty, Unrepeatable, Summary = LDUS.
  • Schedule nesting: Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable ⊂ all. "SCR: Strict is the strongest".
  • Seven schedules: Serial, Complete, Recoverable, Non-recoverable, Cascading, Cascadeless, Strict = SCR NCCS.
  • Serializable test: draw precedence graph; cycle = NOT conflict serializable; no cycle = serializable.
  • 2PL: Grow, peak (lock point), shrink. Conservative = deadlock free; Strict = X locks until commit; Rigorous = all locks until commit.
  • Locks: only S+S is compatible. Sharing is only for readers.
  • Timestamp read: roll back if WTS(A) > TS. Write: roll back if RTS(A) > TS or WTS(A) > TS. A younger one got there first = you roll back.
  • Recovery: Deferred = Redo only (log has new value). Immediate = Undo + Redo (log has old and new).
  • Records per block = block size ÷ record size. Spanned = Splits across blocks; Unspanned = Unwasted? no, Unused space wasted.
  • Dense = every key; Sparse = some keys.

All advantages of a DBMS

  1. Controlling Data Redundancy
  2. Data Consistency
  3. Data Sharing
  4. Data Integration
  5. Integrity Constraints
  6. Data Security
  7. Data Atomicity
  8. Database Access Language
  9. Development of Application
  10. Creating Forms
  11. Report Writers
  12. Control over Concurrency
  13. Backup and Recovery Procedures
  14. Data Independence
  15. Advanced Capabilities

Disadvantages of a DBMS

  1. Cost of Hardware & Software
  2. Cost of Data Conversion
  3. Cost of Staff Training
  4. Appointing Technical Staff
  5. Database Failures

Disadvantages of the file processing system

  1. Data redundancy. The same information is duplicated in several files (e.g. a student's name, roll number and class in both Library and Examinations). It raises storage and access cost.
  2. Data inconsistency. Copies of the same data hold different values; changing a name in the library but not in exams leaves contradictions. Every file holding the item must be changed.
  3. Accessing anomalies (difficulty in accessing data). Needed data cannot be retrieved conveniently or efficiently. Example: the bank officer who wants customers in zip code 600001, then only those with balance of 10,000 or more, needs a new program written each time because the request was not anticipated.
  4. Data isolation. Data is scattered in many files, in different formats, so writing new programs to retrieve the right data is difficult.
  5. Integrity problems. Consistency constraints (e.g. balance never below 500) are coded inside application programs; adding a new constraint means changing many programs.
  6. Atomicity problems. After a failure the data must return to the consistent state before it. Example: transferring 50 from A to B; a crash can remove it from A without crediting B. The transfer must be all or nothing, which is hard in a file system.
  7. Concurrent access anomalies. Many users update at the same time without coordination. Example: account A holds 500; withdrawals of 50 and 100 at about the same time can leave 450 or 400 instead of 350.
  8. Security problems. Not every user should see all data. Programs are added ad hoc, so enforcing it is hard. Example: payroll staff should see employee data but not customer accounts.

Types of conflicts

  1. Lost update (write-write, W-W). Two transactions access the same item and their operations interleave so the item ends up wrong. Example: x=100. T1 reads 100, adds 10; T2 reads 100, subtracts 20; T1 writes 110; T2 writes 80. T1's update is overwritten (correct serial result would be 90).
  2. Dirty read / temporary update (write-read, W-R). A transaction updates an item and then fails (not committed), but another transaction has already read the uncommitted value. Example: x=100; T1 writes x=110; T2 reads 110 and writes 160; T1 fails. T2 used a value that never existed.
  3. Incorrect summary. One transaction computes an aggregate (e.g. a sum) while another updates some of the records, so the aggregate mixes old and new values. Example: A=100, Y=200; T2 sums A (100) then reads Y; T1 changes Y to 300 in between. The sum is wrong.
  4. Unrepeatable read (read-write, R-W). T1 reads an item twice and T2 changes it between the two reads, so T1 sees two different values. Example: A=1000; T1 reads 1000; T2 writes A=3000; T1 reads again and gets 3000.

Types of schedules

  1. Serial schedule. No interleaving of operations of different transactions; always consistent. Example: T1 (R(A), A=A+50, W(A)) completes, then T2 (R(A), A=A+100, W(A)). A=100 gives 150 then 250; T2 then T1 also gives 250. Disadvantages: limits concurrency, wastes CPU, short transactions may wait long.
  2. Complete schedule. The last operation of every transaction is commit or abort. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; T2: R(A) W(A) Abort.
  3. Recoverable schedule. If Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj. Example: T1: R(A), A=A+10, W(A), Commit; then T2: R(A), A=A-5, W(A), Commit.
  4. Non-recoverable schedule. A transaction does a dirty read from an uncommitted transaction and commits before that transaction does. Example: T1 R(x) x=x+10 W(x); T2 R(x) x=x-5 W(x) Commit; T1 fails. T2 should be rolled back but has already committed.
  5. Cascading schedule (cascading rollback). Failure of one transaction forces several dependent transactions to roll back or abort. Example: T1 writes A=A-50; T2 and T3 read that value; T1 fails, so T2 and T3 abort too.
  6. Cascadeless schedule. A transaction may read a value only after the transaction that wrote it commits. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; then T2: R(A) W(A) Commit; then T3: R(A) W(A) Commit.
  7. Strict schedule. A value written by a transaction cannot be read or overwritten by another transaction until the writer commits or aborts. Every strict schedule is recoverable and cascadeless. Example: T1: R(A) W(A) Commit; only then T2: W(A) R(A).

Also know: serializable (equivalent to a serial schedule; conflict or view), non-serial (operations interleaved). Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.
